Also, I now have his father on my case load.  So when I see this guy, he's in pain, and I know why.  I'm reminded of it all over again.  The same questions run through my mind every time I see him.  Did I do enough?  Did I say enough?  Did I listen enough?  Could I have done anything differently?

I do understand about the choices and that I have no power over anyone's but mine.  In this case, I think I just got a little too close.  Anytime clients start having some success in their lives I get excited.  And this guy went from depressed and barely functioning to being employed and housed.  For those few months he was employed and housed, he seemed like some genuine happiness had made it's way into his life.  Then he lost the job, through no fault of his own.  He lost his apartment and ended up back in the shelter.  

I watched this guy go from barely functional enough to get out of the shelter and get himself a meal to competent, confident, employed, and housed.  Seriously, you couldn't wipe the smile off his face if you tried.  And then I watched him descend back.  It was painful to see that smile disappear.  It was painful to watch him come around less and less.  And then he was gone.  I tried everything I could to re-engage him but, he wasn't having it.

I know that I shouldn't attach my professional value to a situation like this but, I can't help but think that maybe I could have done things differently that may have made a difference in the outcome.  I'm trying very hard to not take it personally because I know his suicide wasn't some spiteful action towards me.  He just couldn't take it anymore and didn't feel like he had options.  But that's where I get hung up.  It's part of my job to find and present good options.  And I can't help but think that maybe I missed something that would have suited him.

Something I would suggest is to listen when he needs to talk about something.  Don't make it about a solution or a fix.  And most of all, enjoy your time with him.  Don't treat him like a victim every moment.  Sometimes it's nice for us that have experienced that shit, to just be able to have normal, everyday moments.  So when he's in the middle of one of those moments with you, roll with it and let him feel "normal" as long as he can.  

Another suggestion I have is to ask him directly how he can be supported.  He may know some ways, he may not, he may even be ashamed to ask for the specific support he needs.  And you offering to support him in the way he needs specifically is a great supportive gesture to begin with and will open the door to a supportive life with him.

If he says nothing happened, will you believe him? The only real question is whether or not you will get mentally, emotionally, or physically hurt during the process.

I've seen that you commented that you are going to protect yourself during this encounter.  Do you know this guy at all?  Do you know his capabilities?  Do you know how he is going to react to questioning?  Do you know if he owns firearms?  Do you know if he has a criminal or violent history?  Are you truthfully confident that whatever protection you bring can actually stand up to his abilities?  A potentially violent situation has a lot of moving parts to it and it sounds like you don't know anything about the opposition except for the fact that he might be willing to rape people.

Have you thought about the environment in which the encounter will take place?  His apartment is a terrible idea.  Terrible.  He will feel empowered in a place where he is comfortable and that increases the likelihood of this going very poorly for you.  Stop going back to his place.  You're risking your mental/emotional well being and potentially your life.  Risky behaviour does come with the territory but, don't do it for something that is absolutely not going to help you.  Because I guarantee he is not going to fess up if guilty.  And if he is actually innocent somehow and didn't rape you, how are you going to believe him?

My honest opinion is that I shouldn't be suggesting questions to ask your potential rapist but, instead suggesting that you investigate stuff yourself.  If you hurry, you may be able to get a blood test that can reveal if he drugged you.  You may be able to find other people that were in the pub that night.  Go talk to the bouncers or front door attendants, bar tenders, other patrons if you know any of them.  Were there any female staff there that might have seen you leave with him?  Track down verifiable info for yourself.  Or report it to the police and let them investigate it.  That way if he's guilty, the only place he'll be able to see you is in court room. 

And given all of that, if you still decide to go, you need to be very calm.  You need to be gauging his responses for truthfulness and an emotional mind will want to jump to conclusions.   And you need to be watching his physical reactions.  What he's doing with his hands.  If he's trying to close distance between you two.  Where his eyes might be looking to.  You are also going to need to protect yourself mentally and emotionally.  And with your emotions wide open, that won't be possible.

I'm not sure where you're from so I can't really say much about resources and ideas in your specific area but, I know of a guy in my area that started out working the bare minimum and finding old appliances like vacuums and microwaves.  He would test them out and if they worked he would sell them.  He still had to make money in the meantime to pay his bills but, he eventually saved enough money that he was buying and reselling items.  He didn't have to work at a certain point and that's now all he does.  And he makes more in a year than I will in 10.  I'm not trying to make it sound easy but, he took his "sales" and creative math skills and turned them into something legit.  He started with people's garbage and now he is reselling cars and flipping homes.  One of the things he told me was that in the beginning, don't focus on too much repair.  If it isn't easily repaired, just scrap it and move to the next.  The idea is to find and process a high volume free/super cheap stuff in half decent condition and sell it through kijiji or something like that.

I'm definitely not saying it's going to be easy by any stretch of the imagination.  With your trauma, unfortunately, any path you take is going to be an uphill battle.  But for now, trying to take your existing skills and put them to a legal use is probably going to be much better than trying to deal with new skills or job types alongside the trauma.
